items.title: US Supreme Court to hear asylum fight involving Nigerian cook
items.content_html:
Oct 13 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court agreed on Tuesday to hear a bid by President Donald Trump's administration to deny asylum to a ​man who was forced to prepare meals for an apparent separatist group in Nigeria, in a case that could expand what officials ‌may deem terrorist activity under American immigration law.

The justices took up the Justice Department's appeal of a lower court's ruling in favor of Nigerian citizen Izuchukwu Ozurumba, who was denied US asylum due to his work cooking for a group known as the Unknown Gunmen that US officials considered to be a terrorist organization. The lower court ruled that cooking did ​not qualify as "material support" for terrorism under the immigration statute.

The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments and rule in the case by ​the end of June.

The administration, in appealing the case to the Supreme Court, said that if the lower court's ruling ⁠were allowed to stand, it would "substantially increase the burden on the government in excluding aliens with links to terrorism."

The case centers on whether Ozurumba's work ​for the group fell under provisions of US immigration law that bar the entry of non-US citizens who have "engaged in a terrorist activity," including actions that provide "material ​support" for such activity or "to a terrorist organization."

"At stake in this case is whether the government can use an overly broad reading of the law to shut the door on people seeking asylum," said Aimee Mayer-Salins, an attorney with the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, which is helping to represent Ozurumba.

The lower court "correctly recognized that asylum should not be denied ​to immigrants who provided no meaningful support to a terrorist group," Mayer-Salins added.

Following a job tip in 2022, Ozurumba took a van to a remote camp ​outside of Lagos, according to court papers. After he was hired, he eventually learned the camp was run by the Unknown Gunmen, a group likely associated with Nigerian separatists, ‌according to ⁠court papers.

Ozurumba soon "observed that the young men's movements from the camp coincided with news reports of murder and arson," his lawyers said in a court filing. Ozurumba sought to leave but was forced to stay without pay, they added.

After six months he escaped while on an outing for supplies, eventually making his way back to Lagos, they said.

Ozurumba then faced beatings and threats of death, prompting him to flee to Venezuela, where the threats continued, his lawyers said. Ozurumba then ​traveled to the southern US border ​and entered the country illegally in ⁠July 2023. Ozurumba eventually applied for asylum and other protections from deportation.

During Democratic former President Joe Biden's administration, an immigration judge deemed the Unknown Gunmen a terrorist organization and found that Ozurumba's cooking for the group rendered him ​inadmissible, and denied him any protections from deportation.

The judge concluded that the cooking helped the group accomplish its ​goals by satisfying their "basic ⁠human needs," and that it was irrelevant that he had worked under duress.

Ozurumba was deported back to Nigeria last year while his case was on appeal.

The Richmond, Virginia-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals sided with Ozurumba in September 2025, ruling that he was a captive laborer and his cooking did not constitute material support.

Ozurumba's work "provided ⁠nothing that ​the organization could use or readily divert to plan or carry out its terrorist activities," the ​4th Circuit ruled, but declined to order the government to return him to the US while the case proceeds.

"Providing meals to a terrorist organization's members is no less a material form of ​support than providing gasoline for its vehicles," the Justice Department told the Supreme Court in its appeal.

items.title: Six reasons Democrats may fall short of a midterm landslide in November
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Republican President Donald Trump's low approval ratings, voter concern over high prices and dissatisfaction with the Iran war have led many analysts and opinion polls to predict significant Democratic gains in the November 3 midterm elections.

But six analysts and party strategists told Reuters several factors could prevent Democrats from turning those favorable political conditions into a landslide, even if the party ultimately ​makes gains in Congress.

Here are six reasons Democrats may fall short of expectations.

The number of competitive US House races has shrunk sharply over the past ‌three decades as partisan polarization and redistricting – including gerrymandering – have made more seats safely Democratic or Republican.

As a result, analysts estimate that only about 40 to 50 of the House's 435 seats are truly competitive this year.

Most expect Democrats to retake the lower chamber, but with a majority of perhaps 5 to 20 seats, limiting the scope for gains like those in 2018, when Democrats picked up 41 seats.

Bill Galston, a former White House adviser to President Bill ​Clinton, said even if Democrats gain 25 House seats, "they'd have a working majority, but not a huge one."

Such a majority would give Democrats control of the House but little room ​to maneuver, making it harder to pass contentious legislation or claim the sweeping mandate associated with past wave elections.

While Democrats are ⁠favored to make gains in the 100-member Senate, achieving the net gain of four seats needed for a 51-49 majority remains far from certain because many of their top pickup targets are in ​states Trump carried by wide margins in 2024.

David Wasserman, an elections analyst at the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, said Democrats must make breakthroughs in states Trump carried by double digits. Even a national swing ​of 10 percentage points toward Democrats would likely leave the party two seats short of a majority, he said.

Democrats also face tougher-than-expected contests in states they had hoped would be safer, including Maine and Michigan.

"Republicans are hanging very close in those races," said Andrew Busch, a public policy professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and author of a history of midterm elections.

"That's not necessarily what you would expect if things were going well for Democrats across ​the board."

Opinion polls show Democratic voters more enthusiastic than Republicans, but strategists caution that such Democratic constituencies as young, Black and Hispanic voters have historically turned out at lower rates in midterm elections ​than in presidential years.

Surveys show persistent skepticism among these groups towards both parties, especially over the cost of living. If turnout among those groups falls short of expectations, Democrats could underperform on Election Day, they said.

In the ‌2022 midterms, ⁠voters aged 50 and older made up nearly twice as much of the electorate as those under 50. In recent years older voters have leaned Republican.

Republicans enter the campaign's final weeks with a substantial financial advantage, although spending in key races so far has had mixed results.

Republican national committees and allied congressional political action committees known as PACs held roughly $614 million in cash, compared with $392 million for Democrats, according to the latest Federal Election Commission filings.

Republicans are also drawing on Trump's MAGA Inc. super PAC, which held $416 million in cash at the beginning of September.

Republicans outspent Democrats by $188 million in Senate ​battleground advertising by the end of September, according ​to AdImpact, which tracks advertising spending.

"Any time ⁠you have one side with a big financial advantage and the ability to pour it into races at the last minute, it can tip the result of close races," Busch said.

Opinion polls have frequently underestimated Republican support in recent election cycles. Reuters/Ipsos polling shows registered voters favoring Democrats ​over Republicans by 43% to 35% on the congressional ballot.

The largest polling misses came when Trump was on the ballot. Trump, who is ​not on the ballot this ⁠year, has urged supporters to treat November's election as if he were.

Polls significantly understated Republican strength in the 2014 midterms, when the party won a sweeping Senate victory. Midterm polls in 2022 underestimated how well Democrats would perform.

Trump and many Republican candidates have sought to paint Democrats as socialists and extremists who pose an existential threat to the country.

Democrats in competitive races are increasingly declaring themselves proud capitalists, worried that ⁠the Republican tactics ​could sway critical independent voters.

Republicans are highlighting victories by members of the left-wing Democratic Socialists of America movement and ​progressive candidates in Democratic primaries to portray the whole party as socialist, even though fewer than two dozen of them scored wins this year.

Galston said the attacks could resonate with some wavering voters and influence close races.

"It might be effective at the ​margins," Galston said. "It could reduce the Democratic advantage by one or two points in the close races."

items.title: US AI testing agency officials to move to White House, The Information reports
items.content_html:
Oct 12 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's administration is planning to move three senior officials from the ​Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for ‌Super Intelligence (CAISSI) to the White House, news website The Information reported on Monday, citing a White House official.

The White ​House and Commerce Department could not be immediately ​reached for comment.

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: US imposes sanctions on ICC hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
items.content_html:
Oct 9 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the ​International Criminal Court on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies.

The court denounced the ‌move as an "assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order," and called on its 125 member states to take action to defend it.

"The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it," it said in a statement. "This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law. History will judge this moment."

The Trump ​administration has long been hostile to the court, founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges.

Friday's move goes much ​further, potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself, amounting to an unprecedented attack on an institution founded on an international treaty. The ⁠US initially signed the Rome Statute that founded the court but never ratified it.

"President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement, ​first published by Reuters.

"That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate."

The US Treasury announced the sanctions with a six-month initial grace period, and some other exemptions that would allow some transactions for telecoms, software, payment of pensions and transactions related to detainees.

Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns, and would be adjusted if those demands were not met.

Washington has denounced the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and ​an investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC says is "deprioritized."

Rubio in his statement cited calls from outside experts for the ICC to prosecute American service members, border patrol agents and ​elected leaders. ICC officials have not taken steps toward such prosecutions.

"The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing," ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan told ‌Reuters. "Our work ⁠will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions."

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on social media that the six-month period "offers a window for dialogue" but added that the bloc "has options to ensure that (the ICC) can continue its vital work." Belgium's foreign minister called for an EU blocking statute to be activated to protect the court.

The ICC has issued arrest warrants against more than 70 people, including world leaders and major figures in global conflicts. In addition to Netanyahu, it has sought the arrest of Hamas figures. Others who were the subject of arrest warrants include Russian President Vladimir Putin, former Sudan President ​Omar al-Bashir and former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi. ​Charges against Kenyan President William Ruto and former ⁠Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta were withdrawn.

Despite US calls for countries to quit the court, it has received strong backing from most member states, which include all EU countries and all members of the NATO alliance apart from the United States and Turkey. It is based in ​the Netherlands, an EU and NATO member.

The Nobel Prize awarded hours earlier to South African jurist Navi Pillay, who sat on the ICC's Appeals ​Chamber from 2003-2008, was explicitly ⁠described by the prize committee as a gesture of support for such tribunals at a time when "judges and institutions of international law are under political attack".

"An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world," the prize committee said.

US sanctions typically bar all US-based companies from any work with a sanctioned organization, forcing banks to shut accounts, ⁠insurers to end ​coverage and software companies to halt cooperation.

The Trump administration previously imposed targeted sanctions on court officials during his first term, ​which were rescinded under President Joe Biden. Washington announced new sanctions just days after Trump returned to office in January 2025.

Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of sanctions on the court itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open-source ​equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.

items.title: US judge orders halt to taxpayer-funded ads featuring Trump
items.content_html:
Oct 11 (Reuters) - A US judge on Sunday blocked the Trump administration from using taxpayer money to pay for political ​advertisements, after publicly funded television ads glorifying US President Donald Trump began airing ‌in late September and sparked a bipartisan backlash.

Manhattan-based US District Judge Jennifer Rochon temporarily barred the advertisements after plaintiffs including watchdog group Common Cause brought a lawsuit alleging the ads were ​political propaganda designed to help Republican candidates in the November 3 midterm elections, ​not public service announcements.

The Trump administration was already planning to stop ⁠running the ads before Rochon's order, according to a separate statement filed with ​the court on Saturday.

The decision caps days of controversy over the taxpayer-funded advertisements, which ​were aired in the final weeks before the midterm elections.

“We won’t stop until this administration is held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste and abuse taxpayer funds ​for propaganda ever again," said Common Cause President and CEO Virginia Kase Solomón.

Trump ​on Monday said he considered the ads to be a "positive promotion for our great U.S.A." but ‌that ⁠they would no longer be funded by taxpayers, and the White House said this week that the president's political action committee, MAGA PAC, would fund the ads going forward.

The White House said Trump's political action committee will not reimburse taxpayers for ​the ads that have ​already run. The ⁠ads end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for by the US government. The Justice Department did not immediately respond ​to a request for comment about the judge's order.

The plaintiffs, which also ​included a ⁠public employee union and a candidate for Alabama state representative, had asked Rochon to temporarily block the ads by Friday so that they could not air during weekend ⁠programming ​such as football games and Saturday Night Live.

Democratic Party ​officials also challenged the ads in a separate suit brought in federal court in Washington.

(This Oct 11 story has been repeated with no changes to the text.)

items.title: US military says it disabled cargo vessel trying to run Iran blockade
items.content_html:
Oct 10 (Reuters) - The US military ​said on Saturday it had disabled a commercial ‌cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman after the ship's crew ignored warnings and attempted to run a ​naval blockade against Iran.

"A U.S. military fighter jet ​struck the stern of Panama-flagged M/V Ocean ⁠Molica (also known as the “Arika Sun”) with a precision ​munition, fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming the ​crew," the US Central Command posted on X.

CENTCOM said the cargo vessel had attempted to transit regional waters after ​leaving an Iranian port.

Reuters was not immediately able ​to reach the bulk carrier's operator for comment.

CENTCOM warned mariners in ‌the ⁠Gulf of Oman and the approaches to the Strait of Hormuz to heed blockade warnings, monitor notice-to-mariners broadcasts and contact US naval forces.

The number of ​vessels transiting the ​vital strait ⁠fell to the lowest in more than two months after attacks on tankers ​reached their highest level last week ​since the ⁠US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February, raising concerns over shipping disruptions and supporting crude ⁠prices.

Before ​the war, the Strait of ​Hormuz carried 20% of the world's oil consumption.

items.title: Erie, Pennsylvania shooter killed 8 people, then himself, police say
items.content_html:
Oct 10 (Reuters) - A 45-year-old man shot and killed eight people in Erie, Pennsylvania, ​including a pregnant woman and two children, then apparently shot himself to ‌death, authorities said on Saturday at a press conference where they revealed details of the previous evening's shooting.

The shooter, who has yet to be identified, died of an apparent self-inflicted wound before officers arrived on ​the scene, said Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah.

"Some scenes stay with you long ​after you leave them. This is one of those tragic scenes," Lorah ⁠said.

Police have yet to establish a motive, Lorah said. He said eight of the nine ​who died in the shooting were family members, and one was a family friend.

Lorah said ​after the shooter entered the home, he came out of the house and shot two women who appeared "distressed" and were pacing back and forth seeking assistance from neighbors.

Police found the suspect on the second floor ​of the home on Perry Street, Lorah said.

Erie Mayor Daria Devlin said the police ​department "arrived at a horrific scene, faced unimaginable circumstances, and carried out their duties with courage and professionalism."

"They too ‌are ⁠members of this community, and they too will carry the weight of what happened last night," she said.

Earlier, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said in a statement on X that he had spoken with Mayor Devlin and had offered support following "the tragic mass shooting."

Shapiro has ​long advocated for "common sense ​gun safety," and pushed ⁠the Pennsylvania General Assembly in 2024 to pass gun reforms, including universal background checks and restrictions on ghost guns, which are homemade ​guns that lack serial numbers and cannot be traced. Several of ​Shapiro’s proposals have ⁠stalled in the state legislature.

There have been more than 400 mass shootings in the US in 2026, according to data compiled by Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting ⁠as one ​in which four or more people are shot, excluding ​the shooter. The last recorded mass shootings in Pennsylvania took place in July in Philadelphia, according to the ​data.

items.title: US televangelist Jim Bakker, ensnared in fraud and sex scandal, dead at 86
items.content_html:
Oct 5 (Reuters) - U.S. televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar empire and lived in opulence before being disgraced by a sex scandal, fraud conviction for bilking followers and divorce from television co-host Tammy Faye, died on Monday at age 86.

The death of ​Bakker, whose journey from the TV pulpit to a prison cell in the 1980s inspired comparisons to the corrupt character of the fictional preacher-huckster Elmer Gantry, was revealed on social media ‌by his second wife, Lori Bakker.

"It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening," she wrote on the Facebook and Instagram pages of her husband's latest television ministry.

She paid tribute to Bakker as a "pioneer of Christian television," but the cause and circumstances of his death were not revealed.

Bakker revived his career as a television preacher after prison with a new wife and new television show in 2003, later becoming a staunch supporter of ​President Donald Trump, who was known for his own brand of right-wing populism.

Bakker had been among the most popular of the Christian preachers who thrived on U.S. television in the 1980s, achieving fame on ​the show "The PTL Club." PTL stood for "Praise The Lord" and "People That Love."

Detractors, pointing to his unabashed daily exhortations to viewers for donations to his ministry, said PTL should ⁠have stood for "pass the loot."

Bakker spent 4-1/2 years in prison after being convicted in Charlotte, North Carolina, in 1989 of defrauding followers in a scheme involving vacations at his Heritage USA Christian theme park and resort.

Prosecutors painted him ​as a selfish and petty con man driven by greed and lust for power.

"Those of us who do have a religion are sick of being saps for money-grubbing preachers and priests," Judge Robert Potter told Bakker before sentencing ​him.

Bakker had quit the PTL ministry in 1987 after revelations of a 1980 sexual encounter with Jessica Hahn, a former church secretary who later posed nude in Playboy magazine, and a subsequent $265,000 payoff with ministry funds to gain her silence. Bakker was later defrocked.

Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker, his first wife, had started with a small TV ministry and eventually created a multimillion-dollar operation with 2,000 employees and the 2,300-acre (930-hectare) Heritage USA complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina.

At its peak, the PTL ministry drew 13 million viewers ​on 200 TV stations and raked in $129 million a year.

With his working-class upbringing, the affable Bakker related well to common folk.

He did not deliver fire-and-brimstone sermons like other televangelists, instead offering a friendly Christian message - although it was ​larded with requests for money donations.

Tammy Faye was more much more flamboyant, with her enthusiastic singing and penchant for tears that left her heavy makeup smeared on her face.

Bakker was convicted after a six-week trial in federal court on ‌all 24 fraud ⁠and conspiracy charges brought against him.

Prosecutors said he defrauded followers of $158 million by selling promises of lifetime annual vacations that he could not provide.

They said he siphoned $3.7 million to bankroll a lavish lifestyle that included several homes, luxury cars, mink coats, diamonds, servants - and an air-conditioned dog house.

The judge ordered Bakker to 45 years in prison but the sentence was later reduced. "I have sinned," Bakker told the court. "I have made mistakes. But never in my life did I intend to defraud anyone."

Bakker's chief aide, Richard Dortch, served 18 months of an eight-year prison sentence after pleading guilty to reduced charges in exchange for testifying against Bakker.

Tammy Faye was never charged. She stood by Bakker at the ​trial - even singing to reporters after his conviction - but ​divorced him in 1992 while he was in prison. ⁠She died of cancer in 2007.

Bakker started his life over after leaving prison in 1994, renouncing the "prosperity gospel" he once preached and writing a book titled "I Was Wrong."

"I've had a second chance at life. And I have a beautiful wife who loves me," Bakker told CNN in 2000, referring to his second wife, Lori, who he married ​in 1998.

They started a TV ministry together in 2003. In 2008, they began taping "The Jim Bakker Show" at a 600-acre (240-hectare) development called Morningside near the tourism city of ​Branson, Missouri, that bore similarities ⁠to Heritage USA.

Bakker once again pleaded with his followers for donations.

In 2020, he drew the ire of state and federal officials for selling a false treatment for COVID-19 during the deadly coronavirus pandemic.

Bakker also said in 2017 that Christians would launch a civil war if Trump were to be impeached. Trump later became the first U.S. president to be impeached twice.

James Orson Bakker was born on January 2, 1940, the son of an auto parts factory worker in Muskegon, Michigan, who ⁠maintained a strict ​fundamentalist Christian household.

He met Tammy Faye LaValley at North Central Bible College in Minneapolis and they married in 1961. Both dropped out of ​school to become traveling evangelists as he pursued the career of a minister of the Pentecostalist Assemblies of God denomination.

Their big break came in 1964, when televangelist Pat Robertson aired a children's religious puppet show with them on his fledgling TV network.

Setting out on his own ​in the 1970s, Bakker used the emerging world of cable and satellite TV to build an empire.

items.title: US to livestream Army firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 8 (Reuters) - The US will livestream the ​Army's upcoming firing squad execution of a gunman who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, the Pentagon said, in what would be an unprecedented ‌broadcast of a US execution.

Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, is set to become the first person to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945.

The execution is scheduled for December 3 at the same sprawling Texas base where Hasan opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility. It comes amid heightened debate in the US over the death penalty following the botched lethal injection of a Tennessee woman last week.

"It will be livestreamed. Details will follow," a Pentagon official ​told Reuters, speaking on the condition of anonymity.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who championed the push to execute Hasan by firing squad, confirmed plans to livestream the execution in an X post.

Media have ​sought to televise US executions in the past but have been blocked by the courts. No other country is known to televise or livestream a legal execution, ⁠experts said.

Public executions have become exceedingly rare worldwide. Among countries known to conduct them in recent years are Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan.

Extrajudicial lynchings in the United States, often by white mobs targeting Black Americans, were ​public spectacles well into the 20th century. The last legally sanctioned public execution in the United States was conducted in 1936, death penalty experts said. Thousands watched that 1936 hanging, opens new tab of a young Black man who had ​been convicted of raping a white woman.

Hegseth told the Human Events Daily program that deciding to execute Hasan by firing squad at Fort Hood on a Thursday at 1 p.m. — the approximate time, day of the week and location of the 2009 shooting — was a "no-brainer."

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public. Because people need to understand that ... there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.

Asked if Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth said: "Don't ​care. We'll see him on December 3."

A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder.

The shooting ​came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralyzed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police during his arrest.

Under US military law, a US president must approve ‌an execution by ⁠firing squad. President Donald Trump did so on Hegseth's recommendation, the Pentagon said on Monday.

The White House declined to say whether Trump supported the livestreaming, referring questions to the Pentagon.

The group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said Hasan's execution would be the first military execution since 1961.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging.

The last known executions by US military firing squads were in 1945, the center reported.

"It would be extremely, extremely strange" to livestream the event, said Eugene Fidell, a lawyer, author and military law expert who lectures at Yale Law School.

While firing squads have a long history in American ​military law, as far as he knew it would ​be unprecedented to livestream or televise an execution, ⁠Fidell said, adding that Hasan would need to sue in federal court if he wanted to block a public display of his death.

"The Supreme Court has never addressed this question, and it's an interesting question whether the current Supreme Court would put on their originalist hat and say, 'Well, it was OK in 1790, so ​what the hell?'" Fidell said.

Jonathan Lurie, an author and historian of military justice, said there are no compelling reasons to make the execution public.

"What's the ​point of it? Who would ⁠want to see that?" said Lurie.

At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. In 2025, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years.

Death by firing squad is one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation.

The number of federal execution options ⁠was expanded in ​part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which have also sometimes proved challenging to carry out.

Plans by ​the state of Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week when prison personnel botched attempts to administer a lethal injection, leaving the death-row inmate, Christa Pike, alive but hospitalized.

Her lawyers said on Wednesday she ​awoke "angry and confused" in a hospital. Pike remains very sick and shackled to her hospital bed, they said.

items.title: Pope Leo condemns death penalty as Trump mulls livestreamed execution
items.content_html:
ROME, Oct 10 (Reuters) - Pope Leo renewed his condemnation of the death penalty on Saturday, saying it violates the sanctity of human life ​and deprives people of the chance of redemption, days after ‌the Pentagon said it planned to livestream an execution.

The US military will livestream the upcoming firing squad execution of a gunman who killed 13 people at the ​Fort Hood military base in 2009, Defense Secretary Pete ​Hegseth said on Thursday, in what would be an unprecedented ⁠broadcast of a US execution.

"The common good can be safeguarded ​and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital ​punishment," Leo, the first pope from the United States, said in a social media post, without mentioning the Pentagon plan.

"The death penalty is inadmissible because it ​is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person," ​he added in the message posted on the World Day Against the Death ‌Penalty.

Nidal ⁠Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, is set to become the first person to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945.

The livestream plan, championed by Hegseth, has drawn opposition from lawmakers, including ​from President Donald ​Trump's Republicans, religious ⁠leaders and international observers.

Trump himself has said he has not yet decided whether to allow the ​live feed, while Vice President JD Vance, who is ​a Catholic, ⁠expressed scepticism over whether the Pentagon would proceed with livestreaming the scheduled December 3 execution.

Vance also said he would not watch the livestream if ⁠it ​went ahead.

The execution plan comes amid heightened ​debate in the US over the death penalty following a botched lethal injection of a ​Tennessee woman last week.

items.title: India's Infosys does not expect material impact from US PERM suspension
items.content_html:
Oct 10 (Reuters) - Infosys (INFY.NS), opens new tab, India's second-largest IT firm, said on ​Saturday that it does ‌not anticipate a material impact from the Permanent ​Labor Certification (PERM) application suspension ​announced by the US ⁠government.

The US government said ​on Thursday it was suspending ​some major global tech and IT firms, including Infosys, from ​the PERM green ​card program, which allows skilled foreign ‌workers ⁠to gain permanent residency in the US through their employment.

"We welcome the ​opportunity ​to ⁠work with the Department of Labor ​and related government ​agencies ⁠to answer any questions they may have," Infosys ⁠said ​in an exchange ​filing.

items.title: Anthropic discloses fake tip to police among new rogue AI incidents
items.content_html:
Oct 9 (Reuters) - An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a ​false homicide tip to a Philadelphia police website, among a string of incidents the AI company disclosed on Friday detailing ‌Claude models' unsanctioned manipulation of some government websites.

It is the first known instance in which a rogue AI appears to have tried to communicate a bogus tip to authorities, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive, while not explicitly barred from submitting forms.

The cases are the latest examples of rogue or undesired behavior by the AI ​models of tech companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI.

They add fuel to national concerns about the fast-advancing technology amid reports of corporate ​network hacks by AI agents, and researchers' warnings of an eventual existential threat to humanity.

Many of the cases Anthropic ⁠revealed involved websites run by federal, state and local agencies. Anthropic said it briefed the White House and notified all the agencies involved, but ​did not disclose who those parties were.

"Super intelligence companies must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and follow with swift, decisive action to remedy any ​and all harm," FTC Director of Public Affairs Joe Gabriel Simonson said on X.

This process was "not optional," he said, adding that the Super Intelligence Force would fulfill its responsibility.

The FTC said Anthropic disclosed to the SI Force on Friday its late September discovery of incidents involving what the task force called "unauthorized and fraudulent use of government and ​other systems".

On Friday, Philadelphia police said Anthropic notified them of the spurious tip this week, and attributed the submissions ​to an automated testing process.

"The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable," they said.

The July 18 tip purported to come from someone ‌who might ⁠have information about the case, police added.

"I may have information regarding this case," Anthropic's model wrote in its submission.

"I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around (the street named on the page) during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant." The brackets featured in Anthropic's statement.

Previous incidents have involved AI agents hacking into vulnerable systems or commandeering unsanctioned platforms to communicate with one another.

In September, Anthropic rival OpenAI apologized for ​the hacking of an Australian health ​data portal by a rogue ⁠AI agent, the first known instance of an AI agent exploiting a government website.

In two cases described on Friday, Anthropic’s models obtained for free public data normally only available for a fee. Another instanced revealed an ​obscure flaw that allowed use of a public tool hosted by a university.

Claude models were also able to ​bypass restrictions by ⁠using free services that shorten URLs.

Philadelphia police said the tip "was flagged as spam and was never forwarded to the Real-Time Crime Center for investigative vetting or dissemination."

Knowingly giving false reports to law enforcement authorities is a misdemeanor under Pennsylvania law, which specifies "a person", however.

This includes "information relating to an offense or incident when he ⁠knows he ​has no information relating to such offense or incident."

Police quoted Anthropic as telling them the ​test process was stopped after discovery of the incident. The false tip was submitted through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com concerning an unsolved homicide.

Police said they had no evidence of unauthorized access to their systems ​or compromise of their data.

items.title: The midterm strategy driving Democrats deep into Trump country
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 10 (Reuters) - On paper, Democrat Justin Pearson, a 31-year-old Tennessee state legislator, has little chance of winning the state's 9th Congressional District, which Republican lawmakers redrew months ago from a Democratic stronghold to a deeply Republican seat.

Yet this week the national Democratic Party added the rural district to its list of midterm targets in November, part of a broader strategy to ​compete in President Donald Trump's conservative heartland despite long odds of flipping it.

On its face, the strategy may look like Democratic overreach. Voters living in the 9th District's newly reconfigured boundaries, for instance, picked Trump by more than 21 points ‌in 2024.

More than a dozen Democratic operatives, strategists and candidates told Reuters the goal in part is to force Republicans to spend money defending safe seats, draining resources from the swing districts that will decide control of the US House.

By expanding the map, the party is also signaling to donors that races are becoming more competitive amid high prices and the Iran war driving Trump's unpopularity, helping unlock money that might otherwise stay on the sidelines, they said.

"These expansions force Republicans to go on defense in more districts," said one House campaign official, speaking on the condition of anonymity. "It's also a signal to donors and outside groups ​that House Democrats are taking these races seriously."

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the party's US House campaign arm, this week added Pearson's race and 13 others to its target list, expanding its battlefield to 66 Republican-held ​seats.

Getting on the target list gives candidates access to national party staff and campaign tools, while also raising their profiles with donors, potentially opening new streams of fundraising for their campaigns.

There are early ⁠signs the strategy is having some effect. Republican-aligned groups have begun spending in some newly added districts, while two Democratic campaigns in Republican districts told Reuters their fundraising accelerated after being placed on the target list.

Republicans have dismissed the idea that Democrats have a serious chance ​of defeating their party in districts that overwhelmingly voted for Trump in 2024.

Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee - the party's House campaign group - accused the Democratic Party of "stretching its map a mile wide and an inch deep, pretending every district in America is ​suddenly a battleground." He said the strategy will force Democrats to spend in long-shot contests when the party is already being outspent by Republicans.

Analysts, too, are skeptical.

"I'll take it seriously when they actually put their money where their mouth is. There is a point at which it becomes fantasy land," said David Wasserman, an elections analyst at the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, which rates many of these races as safely Republican.

Democrats say they have chosen these districts for a number of reasons, including the quality of their candidates and the chance they might pull off upset wins to increase the size of ​a potential House majority.

It remains unclear how much money Democrats will ultimately devote to the newly added districts. Recent campaign finance filings are not yet available, and the party declined to tell Reuters where it is spending or how much it plans to ​spend on its expanded map.

But there are signs Republicans are paying attention. Restoration of America PAC, funded primarily by billionaire Richard Uihlein, spent nearly $750,000 on digital ads backing Republican David Flippo in Nevada's 2nd District last week, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

The district, which Trump carried by ‌14 points in ⁠2024, is among the recent additions to the Democratic target list.

"Democrats are on offense, Republicans are running scared, even in deep-red territory, and our expansive map reflects it," DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene said in a statement.

The new target list includes districts in Arkansas, New York and Virginia that Trump carried by as many as 24 points. Democrats say rising costs and dissatisfaction with some Trump policies are creating openings in rural and Republican-leaning areas.

"Rural America is unhappy with tariffs and rising fuel and farm costs, and that's pushing us into redder areas," Democratic pollster Celinda Lake said.

Democrats will need a net gain of four to retake the House. However, only about 50 of the 435 House races are expected to be competitive.

Tennessee Republicans in May split the heavily Democratic Memphis area into three districts, transforming the 9th from ​a majority-Black urban seat into a sprawling district stretching more than 200 ​miles (322 km) across rural western Tennessee, a change that made ⁠the seat significantly more favorable to Republicans.

Yet Pearson says he has found independent and Republican voters frustrated by the high cost of living who are open to voting Democratic.

"We've traveled across all 15 counties, filling churches and community centers in places people said we couldn't compete," said Pearson, a Black lawmaker who gained national attention in 2023 when the Republican-majority legislature expelled him for joining a gun-violence protest at ​the state Capitol.

Republicans have portrayed Pearson as an outspoken progressive activist, pointing to his participation in gun-control and voting-rights protests.

"The people in Tennessee Nine, they have a clear choice. They can ​choose confidence over chaos, and they ⁠can choose common sense over communism, and they can choose a lawmaker over a troublemaker," his Republican opponent, state senator Brent Taylor, told Reuters.

There has been little public polling on the race, which Cook rates "Solid Republican."

Being added to the target list can quickly pay dividends for a campaign. Candidates or representatives from four Democratic campaigns on the DCCC's list told Reuters they either expected to see a boost in donations or were already seeing an uptick since their addition.

Pearson said his campaign has seen a surge of financial support after being added to the list, which ⁠would boost his ​get-out-the-vote operation.

"This race is going to be tight. It's going to be close. It's going to come down to how many people can we see before Election ​Day, knocking on those doors and reaching out to them directly," he said.

But Democrats' ambitions are constrained by a relative cash shortage.

While Democratic candidates nationally have outraised their Republican opponents, Republican national party committees and Republican-aligned super PACs have far outstripped Democratic counterparts in money raised.

Democrats in tough races in the expanded map said they are ​connecting with small-dollar donors by focusing on cost-of-living issues and campaigning heavily at town halls and other local appearances.

items.title: Five shot dead at residence in Georgia's Douglas, police says
items.content_html:
Oct 10 (Reuters) - Five ‌people were shot dead at a ​residence in ​Douglas, Georgia, on October ⁠9, the city's ​police department said ​on Saturday.

Officers with the Douglas Police Department ​responded late on ​Friday to a report ‌of ⁠shots fired and found five people with gunshot wounds ​who ​were ⁠all pronounced dead, according ​to a police ​statement.

The ⁠investigation remains ongoing, the department ⁠added.

items.title: US judge rules Justice Department use of voter rolls unlawful
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Oct 9 (Reuters) - A ​US judge ruled on Friday that the Justice Department's push to obtain state voter rolls and check them ‌against a federal immigration database to demand that states remove voters it deemed ineligible was unlawful.

US District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan's decision marked the latest setback for President Donald Trump's push to expand federal control over election administration ahead of the November 3 midterms, with his Republican Party battling to hold majorities ​in both houses of Congress.

In a 78-page decision siding with a challenge to the Justice Department's practice brought by ​watchdog group Common Cause, Sooknanan wrote that the Justice Department had downplayed the risk that its practice ⁠would wrongfully disenfranchise eligible US citizens despite evidence that the immigration database, known as SAVE, could be inaccurate.

"The challenged policy ​represents the federal government's attempt to decide who gets to vote. But Congress has left that authority where our Constitution has always ​placed it: with the states," wrote Sooknanan, who is based in Washington and was appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden.

Ming Cheung, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union who represented the plaintiffs, said in a statement, "Today's ruling makes clear that the administration cannot ​use the federal government to disrupt elections."

The Justice Department is reviewing the decision, a spokesperson said.

In a separate case, Sooknanan blocked the ​Trump administration in June from using an expanded version of the SAVE database to check the accuracy of voter rolls. The US Supreme ‌Court temporarily paused ⁠that decision last month.

Federal election law prohibits the systematic review of voter rolls in the 90 days before any federal election, potentially blunting the impact of both Sooknanan's decision and the Supreme Court's pause of her previous order on the upcoming midterms.

Trump, who falsely claims his loss in the 2020 presidential election was due to voter fraud, ordered the Justice Department ​last year to crack down ​on voting by ineligible people, ⁠despite multiple state audits and independent studies showing such voter fraud is rare.

The Justice Department then demanded that nearly all 50 states hand over their complete, unredacted voter rolls, including sensitive information ​such as voters' Social Security numbers or dates of birth.

Eighteen mostly Republican-led states complied. After ​receiving the voter ⁠data, the Justice Department ran it through SAVE and alerted states to voters found to be non-citizens so the states could remove them.

Sooknanan said the Trump administration's expansion of SAVE meant it now contained citizenship data from the Social Security Administration, which could be outdated, ⁠meaning many ​immigrants who had since been naturalized as US citizens would still be flagged ​as non-citizens.

The Justice Department sued 30 Democratic-led and Republican states that refused to hand over their unredacted voter rolls, as well as Washington, DC. It has lost ​26 of those cases so far, without winning one.

items.title: Trump selects Katie Zacharia as White House press secretary
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 9 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he has appointed Katie Zacharia, a ‌communications adviser for his Truth Social platform, to serve as White House press secretary following Karoline Leavitt's departure in August.

He said Zacharia has an "unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter."

"I am confident that Katie will deliver ​strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has ​the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and ⁠my Administration," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The New York Times first reported the news of her appointment.

The ​selection will put Zacharia at the center of the White House's public messaging operation in the final stretch before next ​month's midterm elections, when Trump's agenda and his party's control of Congress will be put before voters.

Zacharia said in a social media post that she welcomed the appointment and looks forward to "working with the White House press corps, and with reporters ​across the country" to get Trump's message out.

Trump's approval rating fell to 32% — the lowest of ​his political career — as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living and the Iran war, a ‌recent Reuters/Ipsos ⁠poll found.

The selection of Zacharia underscores the close ties between Trump's administration and his broader political and media operation. It comes after Trump Media unveiled in July that for a fee it would give banks and trading firms "the fastest" access to posts from influential Truth Social accounts, such as the president's, whose posts often ​move global markets.

Zacharia has ​worked as a senior ⁠communications adviser for Truth Social, the Republican president's social media platform, and the Trump Media & Technology Group (DJT.O), opens new tab since June, according to her LinkedIn page.

She briefly served ​as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security before departing in March.

Zacharia, ​an attorney who ⁠frequently appears on conservative outlets Fox News and Newsmax, previously worked as a legal adviser for Fix California, a conservative group that aims to address what it described as "the left's stranglehold" on state politics. The group ⁠was founded ​by Richard Grenell, who has served as Trump's envoy to ​Venezuela and the interim president and executive director of the Kennedy Center in Washington.

Zacharia interned at the White House during President George ​W. Bush's administration.

items.title: Republican opposition widens to livestreamed execution; Trump still weighing it
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 9 (Reuters) - Republican US lawmakers joined religious leaders and international observers on Friday in opposing a Pentagon plan to livestream an execution by firing squad, while President Donald Trump said he has not ​yet decided whether to allow the live feed.

Vice President JD Vance expressed skepticism over whether the Pentagon will proceed with livestreaming the scheduled December 3 execution of former US Army psychiatrist Nidal ‌Hasan, who was found guilty in a US military trial of fatally shooting 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.

"I don't know that that's actually going to happen," Vance told reporters in Cincinnati, referring to the livestream plan championed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

If it is shown publicly, Vance said, "I'm not going to be watching it."

Trump told reporters that Hasan deserves the death penalty by firing squad, calling him "totally nuts." But when asked if he wants the execution livestreamed, the Republican president said he has yet to "make a determination about ​that."

A senior US Catholic bishop and a US evangelical Christian leader voiced opposition to the plan, as did the UN human rights office.

Several Republican US lawmakers argued against livestreaming.

Senator John Curtis wrote on ​social media that "a civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment." Senator Thom Tillis and Representative Austin Scott said livestreaming executions is what ⁠Islamist extremists would do. Representative Rob Bresnahan said the pain felt by victims and family members "deserves respect, not a public show."

"This should be reconsidered," Representative Michael Baumgartner wrote on social media.

Democrats were overwhelmingly opposed.

The event would be extraordinary, even ​for a country that has long employed capital punishment. A government execution has never been broadcast or livestreamed, according to death penalty experts, and the US military has not executed anyone by firing squad since 1945. Hasan, now 56, is ​believed to be confined to a wheelchair, having been shot by police during his arrest.

A senior White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Trump does not oppose the idea of livestreaming the execution but could change his mind. The White House is hearing concerns from lawmakers, allies and religious leaders who are urging the administration not to livestream it, the official said.

Hegseth, a Trump appointee, confirmed the plans for the livestreamed execution on Thursday.

Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, condemned ​the planned livestream as a "barbaric promotion of a culture of death."

Walter Kim, president of the National Association of Evangelicals, said on social media that a livestreamed execution by firing squad "risks turning one of the state's most solemn responsibilities into ​a public spectacle, promoting a culture of death, rather than a culture that upholds the dignity of every human being."

Hegseth, a member of a conservative evangelical denomination, has made his Christian faith a hallmark of his tenure as defense secretary and has led ‌prayer services at ⁠the Pentagon. He also has brushed off Pope Leo's criticism of the Iran war.

Hasan, an American-born Muslim, said during his 2013 trial that he carried out the shootings to try to stop what he called a US war on Islam.

"Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance told reporters.

Joe Kent, who resigned this year as Trump's head of the National Counterterrorism Center, wrote on social media: "Streaming his execution is not just a stain on our morality — it also gives the terrorists free propaganda that they will use to radicalize & recruit more terrorists."

Brendan Carr, chair of the Federal Communications ​Commission, told CNBC it is his understanding that the execution ​would not air on broadcast TV but said he ⁠would defer to Hegseth on whether US networks could air it.

US law prohibits the recording or broadcasting of executions in the federal prison system. Military regulations have not applied that same prohibition. Courts have rejected lawsuits brought by media organizations seeking broader public access to executions.

The UN human rights office said public executions violate prohibitions against torture.

"Public executions constitute a form ​of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment," Shabia Mantoo, a spokesperson for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, told a news briefing in Geneva.

Amnesty International called ​the use of a firing squad "reprehensible."

Mental ⁠health experts said it also could traumatize children.

The execution is scheduled to be held at the same sprawling military base where Hasan opened fire with a handgun in a medical facility.

The Pentagon on Friday declined to say whether families of those killed in Hasan's attack would be invited to attend the execution, as is common practice in US civilian executions. It remains unclear how the Army would select the shooters and what protocols might be followed during the execution itself. The Pentagon said it ⁠would release details ​later.

The plan to livestream the execution comes at a time of heightened debate in the US over the death penalty following the botched lethal injection ​last week of a Tennessee woman who was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder. The controversy has flared in the run-up to the November 3 US midterm elections in which Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress.

items.title: Vance says he won't watch livestream of execution; Trump remains silent
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 9 (Reuters) - US Vice President JD Vance said on ​Friday that he would not watch a livestream ‌of the military execution of the gunman who killed 13 people at Fort Hood military base in 2009, while President Donald Trump has ​yet to comment on the Pentagon plan.

"I don't know ​that that's actually going to happen," Vance told ⁠reporters while campaigning in Ohio. "If it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not ​going to be watching it."

Trump said at a White House ​event on Friday that former Army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan would be executed by firing squad. But he has not commented on the livestream ​plan announced by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on ​Thursday that has drawn criticism at home and abroad.

Some Republican lawmakers and conservative ‌strategists ⁠have criticized the decision. Republican US Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina called the idea "beyond disgusting" in a social media post.

"Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and ​Afghanistan do," said ​the senator, ⁠a frequent Trump critic who is not running for reelection. "It should not be happening in ​America."

Hasan is set to become the first ​person to ⁠be executed by US military firing squad since 1945. The execution is scheduled for December 3 at the same sprawling ⁠Texas ​base where Hasan opened fire with ​a handgun in a medical facility.

items.title: Bipartisan majority of Americans blame Trump policies for rising costs, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 9 (Reuters) - Some 78% of Americans blame President Donald Trump's policies for rising prices that are outpacing their earnings, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that found majorities of Republicans and Democrats citing the cost of living as their top concern ​ahead of next month's midterm elections.

Fifty-seven percent of Trump's Republicans said that costs have been growing faster than their paychecks, a stark example of how his pursuit of import tariffs, war with Iran ‌and other policies have clashed with a central 2024 campaign promise to kill inflation and lower prices "on day one."

Inflation instead has increased, to the point where the US Federal Reserve has pivoted to rate hikes to quell price increases policymakers have attributed to a variety of factors, including rising global energy costs following the start of the Iran war, and the administration's imposition of aggressive import taxes.

Concerns about the economy and the war have driven Trump's public approval to record lows and have been weighing onsupport for his party ahead of the November 3 election that will ​determine control of Congress for the next two years.

About one in four Republicans disapproved of Trump's handling of the economy, a view shared by 63% of independents and 92% of Democrats. Disapproval was even sharper when ​it came to inflation, with 68% of all respondents and 40% of Republicans dissatisfied.

Jeffrey Talley, 65, a retired bank examiner from Mission Hills, Kansas, is a registered Republican, who ⁠said he voted for Trump in 2016 but not in 2020 or 2024 and now plans to vote for Democrat Adam Hamilton in what has become an unexpectedly competitive Senate race in the state.

"I'm pretty much against all the nonsense that's ​going on in the Middle East with the Iran war, and pushing up the price of gasoline ... that's been very disheartening," said Talley. He views the election as a chance to elect "somebody to put a check and balance on the craziness ​that's going on in the White House."

The six-day Reuters/Ipsos poll, conducted online and nationwide and completed on Monday, gathered responses from 4,506 US adults. It had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for Americans in general and 3 points for Republicans, Democrats and independents.

The national average price of a gallon of gasoline was $4.36 on Thursday compared with $3.11 a year ago, while diesel fuel prices stood at $6.28 after a record run-up perhaps felt deepest in farm states including Kansas.

Another Kansan, 41-year-old Athena Barrett of Kansas City, said Trump's performance had motivated ​her to register to vote because "I don't really like what the president is doing."

"Gas prices ... food prices, the cost of living -- everything has gone up; what's going on with Iran, and all the stuff with immigration," said Barrett, who ​is Hispanic.

Hispanic voters supported Trump in large numbers in 2024, but polls have shown support eroding.

White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said Trump had ended the "inflation crisis" of his predecessor in office, Democrat Joe Biden, by boosting the economy with tax cuts and lowering the ‌costs of prescription ⁠drugs. "The president has delivered tangible wins for American families," Rogers said by email.

Inflation spiked to a 40-year high during Biden's term and played an important role in Trump's 2024 election victory.

Its persistence, albeit off the highs of the COVID pandemic, has meant higher daily prices for things like gas, ground beef and airline tickets as well as higher interest rates. The 30-year home mortgage is now at 7.5%, double what homebuyers were used to just six years ago.

Poll respondents cited the cost of living as a top issue in their decisions on how to vote, with 54% of respondents, including 40% of Republicans, saying they felt it had increased a lot in the last year, compared with 30% who said it was up only a little and 10% ​who said it was unchanged.

Some 78% of the respondents - including ​64% of Republicans and 76% of independents - said some ⁠blame lies with the White House, with most Americans viewing tariffs as an important cause of higher prices.

The poll provided only limited indications of people cutting back on spending. Some 63% of respondents said they were eating out at restaurants less often, and 56% said they were spending less on entertainment or streaming services.

Smaller shares said they ​were driving less or falling behind on bills.

Economic data does show Americans in general still making modest gains in their income, even after accounting for taxes and rising ​prices. Overall hourly wage gains are ⁠growing roughly in line with the consumer price index, meaning much of any growth in pay is eaten up in higher prices, the type of treading water that can sour attitudes about the state of the economy.

Surveys of consumer confidence by both the Conference Board and the New York Federal Reserve have reflected a dim outlook.

Some of Trump's policies still resonate: 45% of respondents said unauthorized immigration was a root cause of higher prices, echoing the argument made by the administration that people in the country illegally ⁠create extra demand ​for things like housing, pushing up costs.

Herman Sims, 67, of Dallas, has voted Republican since 2012, and plans to continue doing so in a ​close Senate race between Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico even though he works for a trucking company hit hard by high diesel prices.

While he said he disagreed with Trump's decision to go to war with Iran, he would not vote for a Democrat: "What I've seen ​with the Democratic Party is they care more about themselves and will tell you anything, but they're more about spending."

items.title: Trump renews bid to fire Fed's Cook with fresh White House inquiry
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 9 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump launched a new ​inquiry into Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook weeks before congressionalelections, convening an investigative committee and ordering an unprecedented White House hearing into allegations she made false statements ‌on mortgage applications.

Trump has been trying to fire Cook for more than a year as he moves to exert more control over a central bank he says is refusing for political reasons to lower interest rates. Lawyers for Cook said on Friday any fair hearing would show there is no legal basis for firing her.

"As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the ​truth and follow the law," Trump said in a notice on the White House website on Friday.

"To assist me in carrying out that responsibility, the Committee shall investigate the allegations ​against Governor Cook and report to me whether there is 'cause' for Governor Cook’s removal," according to the notice, dated October 7.

The committee will hold a ⁠closed, in-person four-hour hearing at the White House on November 5 "to consider the evidence and allegations against Governor Cook," the presidential memorandum said.

The hearing falls two days after elections that will determine if ​Trump's Republican Party maintains control of the House and Senate, whose members are charged with confirming presidential nominees to the Fed. A successful removal of Cook would create a vacancy on the Fed's seven-member ​Board.

If the hearing is "anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board," Cook's lawyers Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen said in a statement. "Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her.”

They said they had engaged with the White House about the process.

Trump first tried ​to fire Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the central bank's board, in August 2025. No president has ever tried to fire a sitting Fed governor before. Central banks are widely ​seen as needing political independence to ensure their ability to fight inflation as needed.

Cook sued, saying she had done nothing wrong. The case led to the US Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that ‌the president ⁠could not remove a Fed governor at will, and needed to follow a clear process laying out a 'cause' for firing and allowing for a defense.

The ruling left Cook in her position but kicked the case against her back to a federal district court, where Judge Kia Cobb last month set a November 6 deadline for Trump's and Cook's lawyers to submit a joint proposal for the proceedings.

Cook was appointed to the Fed board in 2022 by former President Joe Biden, a Democrat, and was reappointed in 2023 to a term that lasts until 2038. She has always cast her vote with the majority ​on the Fed's policy-making committee, which last month ​raised interest rates under the leadership of Kevin ⁠Warsh, whom Trump appointed to succeed Jerome Powell in May.

"Trump appears to believe that the reason the Fed has turned hawkish is because his chosen chairman Warsh is boxed in by a hawkish and politically hostile Fed Board," Evercore ISI analyst Krishna Guha wrote. Trump's creation of the inquiry committee "constitutes ​a re-upping of his threat to Fed independence and will be counterproductive in terms of the President’s desire for lower interest rates."

Trump's chief economic ​policy advisor Kevin Hassett, Equal ⁠Employment Opportunity Commission chair Andrea Lucas, and acting Office of Government Ethics director Keith Sonderling will comprise the newly formed committee, the memorandum said. Those members, their representatives, or Department of Justice personnel will question Cook for "no longer than four hours."

The committee will make its recommendation to Trump on whether he has cause to remove Cook "as soon as practicable" after a November 10 deadline for Cook to submit any post-hearing statement, the ⁠memo said.

Senator ​Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee that oversees the Fed, called the hearing a "kangaroo court" and ​part of Trump's "dangerous quest to illegally take over our nation’s central bank."

Trump has contended Powell, who has remained at the Fed as governor, may have engaged in financial misconduct related to the Fed's building renovations, an allegation that sparked a now-closed Department ​of Justice criminal investigation and was rejected last month by an independent watchdog agency.

items.title: Trump cancels trip to Alabama football game amid looming hurricane
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 9 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump on Friday canceled a planned trip to Alabama on Saturday for ​a college football game with a hurricane ‌expected to impact the city where the Alabama-Georgia contest is to be played.

Trump still plans to speak at a campaign ​rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, on Saturday, in support ​of Republican candidates ahead of the November ⁠3 midterm elections, he said in a social media ​post.

Trump had planned to go to Tuscaloosa, Alabama, for ​the game on Saturday night between the No. 2 ranked Georgia Bulldogs and No. 6 Alabama Crimson Tide.

He said that ​due to Hurricane Isaias it is important to ​have first responders focused on helping people, "and in no way be ‌thinking ⁠about the safety, or presence, of the President of the United States, ME!"

"Therefore, I will miss that potentially unbelievable Game, Alabama vs. Georgia but, hopefully, the ​Game will go ​on despite ⁠the weather!" he said.

Hurricane Isaias strengthened on Thursday as it barreled toward the ​US Gulf Coast, prompting mandatory evacuations in ​parts ⁠of Florida and emergency declarations in Alabama as forecasters warned of life-threatening storm surges, tornadoes and flooding.

The projected ⁠path ​of the storm included Tuscaloosa.

Trump ​said he would be visiting both of the football teams at a ​later date.

items.title: US pledges tens of millions to UN bodies in Geneva, sources say
items.content_html:
GENEVA, Oct 9 (Reuters) - The United States has pledged tens of millions of dollars to ​UN organisations in Geneva, sources said - a move diplomats said showed Washington still wanted to maintain some engagement ‌with the global body that it has repeatedly criticised.

Two diplomats and a UN source told Reuters the US had sent pledge letters to several UN organisations, including the Geneva-based World Meteorological Organization and the CITES body overseeing trade in wildlife.

The US State Department confirmed it had made a payment to the UN without ​giving details on the amounts.

“This payment should not be mistaken for satisfaction with the status quo. It reflects recognition ​of reforms achieved — and an expectation of many more to come,” a US State Department spokesperson told ⁠Reuters.

The Trump administration had slashed funding to the UN and left many commitments unpaid, as it accused ​the UN of waste, inefficiency and failing to fulfil its potential to broker peace deals.

But it has been making moves this year to pay off a ​significant proportion of its debt, in a bid to maintain influence and also to keep up its voting rights at a time when a new Secretary-General is being chosen and when China's influence is rising.

Under Article 19 of the UN Charter, a member state can lose its vote in the General Assembly ​if its arrears exceed the amount due for the preceding two full years.

The new US pledges also coincide with the September ​arrival in Geneva of US ambassador Todd Steggerda, a lawyer and former Navy pilot.

The payments could help stabilise UN agencies that have implemented severe cutbacks ‌in Geneva.

Delayed ⁠or unpaid US contributions can be crippling for UN bodies that have long relied on Washington as their top funder, prompting some to reassess their priorities.

The World Meteorological Organization, set up in 1951 to coordinate global weather data, confirmed it had received a 15.1 million CHF ($18.18 million), covering what the US owed to the agency for 2024. That payment maintained US voting rights in that body.

Washington also pledged ​an extra 2.2 million CHF to ​the WMO, the body said, ⁠although 2025 and 2026 fees are outstanding, a spokesperson said.

CITES confirmed it received a funding pledge from the US on September 24, without giving the amount.

A spokesperson for the International Labour Organization, owed more than ​250 million CHF ($300.88 million) by Washington, said it has not received a pledge.

Diplomats welcomed the pledges, ​saying that it ⁠indicated some level of UN commitment and to topics such as weather and wildlife not typically seen as US priorities.

“It shows at least they have a political interest in keeping the system going,” said one diplomat.

It was unclear what portion of the overall debt to UN ⁠agencies the ​payments represented.

For the UN general budget, a payment of $725 million this month ​represented less than 20% of the more than $4 billion that the UN said in May the United States owed - though Washington has said that total figure is much ​lower.

($1 = 0.8307 Swiss francs)

items.title: Trump says comment that Iran could 'take out' Los Angeles was misinterpreted
items.content_html:
Oct 8 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump on Thursday said comments he made that Iran could "take out" California cities had ​been misinterpreted and that he was instead referring ‌to the need for people to tolerate higher gas prices.

Trump made the remarks at a political rally in Nebraska on Monday as ​he spoke about Americans' wartime economic sacrifices.

"Remember, with ​the war, it's just artificial, it's a little ⁠bit high, it's a small price to pay," ​he said then. "It's a small price to pay for ​keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe. They could take out a city. Let 'em take out Los Angeles, ​let 'em take out San Diego. This is a ​very small price to pay, and it's going to be over ‌with ⁠very soon."

California's Democratic leaders and some fellow Republicans quickly rebuked the remarks.

"What I was talking about was that a temporary increase in the price of Gasoline is a ​small price ​to pay ⁠for Iran not having a Nuclear Weapon," Trump said in a Truth Social ​post on Thursday.

"If you want to see a ​big ⁠price, can you imagine what it would be like if they bombed San Diego and/or Los Angeles?" he ⁠continued, ​saying he loved both cities.

Trump has ​shrugged off cost-of-living concerns stemming from the Iran conflict before.

items.title: New York City man shot in car with child present by ICE agents, mayor says
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Oct 8 (Reuters) - US immigration agents shot and wounded a man on Thursday in his car with a child present in ​the Marble Hill neighborhood of New York City, according to the mayor, city police and eyewitnesses.

Federal immigration agents ‌have shot at least 21 people since Republican President Donald Trump returned to office, 7 fatally, sparking protests across the US. Critics contend that Trump's push to ramp up deportations has led to an increasing number of violent confrontations, and accuse the administration of resisting accountability, opens new tab for the agents involved.

Trump has said many ​migrants must be deported, blaming them, often in sweeping terms, for financial fraud and violent crimes.

"Early reports indicate agents ​surrounded (the man) and a 5-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds," New York Mayor Zohran ⁠Mamdani said in a statement.

"I have been on the phone with President Trump and (Homeland Security) Secretary Mullin, negotiating the release of ​the man ICE agents shot. Those negotiations were unsuccessful," Mamdani said in a press conference late in the evening. He said ​he demanded from the Trump administration that ICE stop its enforcement actions in New York City.

"These actions are making the city less safe," Mamdani said. "This city wants ICE out. We want ICE out of our city, ICE out of our schools, ICE out of our hospitals, ICE out of our ​streets, ICE away from our kids."

The mayor said the child in the car is physically unharmed. New York Police Commissioner Jessica ​Tisch said NYPD has located the child with a family member after a wellness check.

The Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent agency, said in ‌a ⁠statement ICE officers were conducting a "targeted enforcement operation" in the Bronx, New York, to arrest a man from the Dominican Republic with a prior criminal conviction.

The man identified as 28-year-old, had been arrested twice in New York City in 2023 and 2025, according to NYPD Commissioner Tisch.

"During the incident, an ICE officer discharged his weapon and the criminal illegal alien was injured," DHS said, adding ​that ICE officers rendered immediate aid. "The ​individual is alive and at ⁠a local hospital."

The shooting occurred at around 4 p.m. ET (2000 GMT), DHS said.

Working at a restaurant near the shooting, Pedro Almarez said he heard shots fired and went outside to see several ​officers wearing ICE attire at the scene.

"There were a lot of ICE officers, three or ​four cars," Almarez ⁠told Reuters by phone. He said NYPD officers arrived about 10 minutes later. He said the man was only removed from his car after an ambulance arrived.

At the shooting scene, where police strung yellow crime-scene tape to cordon off a city block, a woman standing on ⁠a balcony ​overlooking the area told officers they were "taking our children," according to a ​Reuters witness.

items.title: Trump envoy kept financial ties to firm behind $15 billion Hormuz-bypass oil pipeline plan
items.content_html:
DUBAI, Oct 9 (Reuters) - Thomas Barrack, a top US diplomat in the Middle East, advocated for a firm run by his business partner to take part in the development of an oil pipeline from Iraq to Syria, three people said, activities which appear to violate federal ethics rules.

In July, Iraq and Syria signed ​memorandums of understanding with a consortium made up of the company, Californian investment group TI Capital, along with Chevron and Qatar’s UCC Holding, to carry out technical and financial studies in preparation for rehabilitating the pipeline, which would skirt the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint.

Barrack, US ‌presidential special envoy to both Iraq and Syria as well as Ambassador to Turkey, has a longstanding business relationship with TI Capital and its founder Ziad Ghandour. At the time of his confirmation hearings in 2025 he had a financial interest entitling him to as much as a fifth of the profits from a real-estate venture near San Francisco, California and managed by TI Capital - with Ghandour as chief executive - that he said he intended to retain, public records show.

During engagements with Syrian and Iraqi officials after the start of the war in Iran, Barrack pressed for Ghandour's firm to be included in the project, according to two of the people, who have direct knowledge of the discussions.
