On June 16, a month before the consortium agreement was signed, ​Barrack and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi issued a joint statement that commended Iraq's decision "to advance a memorandum of understanding with TI Capital to rehabilitate the Kirkuk-Baniyas Pipeline." The statement made no mention of Chevron or UCC in connection with the pipeline.

Reuters found no evidence that Barrack stands to ​profit from the pipeline or other projects. His ties to Ghandour would not constitute a criminal conflict of interest unless he stood to directly profit from the pipeline itself, two ethics lawyers told Reuters.

However, Barrack's relationship with Ghandour makes ⁠such advocacy "a serious problem" under the regulation that prohibits officials from participating in matters that call into question their impartiality because of a personal or business relationship, said Richard Painter, a former chief White House ethics lawyer and a professor at the University of Minnesota Law School.

The impartiality rule, which is not a criminal statute, ​can be triggered by the involvement of a business associate in a project, regardless of whether the official has a financial interest of his own.

“The ethical concern is the appearance of a conflict of interest," said Ann Skeet, interim executive director at the Markkula Center for Applied Ethics in Santa Clara University.

Asked what Barrack would ​have needed to do to comply, Painter said: "Have nothing to do with this pipeline. Completely recuse. Say this is not a matter I participate in."

Don Fox, a former general counsel and acting director of the US Office of Government Ethics, said that promotion of TI Capital by Barrack would additionally violate a regulation prohibiting officials from using their office to endorse any enterprise or for the private gain of people they are affiliated with.

Barrack has not filed a conflict-of-interest waiver with the US Office of Government Ethics regarding his ties to the company as it participates in the project, according to a Reuters records request. Waivers allow officials with potential conflicts of interest to participate in matters that would otherwise require the employee be recused.

In a ​signed ethics agreement before his confirmation hearings last year, he committed to recusing himself from matters directly affecting the financial interests of the real-estate venture unless he first obtained such a waiver.

Barrack’s office and Chevron declined to comment. TI Capital, Ghandour and UCC did not respond to requests for comment.

In a July 17 post ​on X, Barrack said the involvement of US companies in Iraq and Syria was “a new paradigm” aimed at bringing clarity and opportunity to the region.

A fourth ethics lawyer said it was up to the State Department to decide whether its employee's financial holdings create a potential conflict of interest.

"Ambassador Barrack has no affiliation with, role in, or financial interest ‌in the Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline ⁠project," a State Department spokesperson told Reuters, while acknowledging Barrack’s relationship with the TI Capital real-estate venture.

His public comments on the pipeline reflect "long-standing, publicly stated US policy interest in regional energy integration," the spokesperson said, adding that Barrack was certified to be in compliance with ethics rules.

In a financial disclosure filed with the US Office of Government Ethics in March 2025, before assuming his diplomatic roles, Barrack declared an equity stake in ACD-TI Oakley Investment LLC, a venture building a large housing project near San Francisco. The filing did not disclose the size of the stake, but said he was entitled to 20% of the company’s profits when the earnings reach an established minimum.

ACD-TI is managed by TI Capital and headed by Ghandour, California state corporate records show. Reuters was unable to find contact details for a company representative, and did not get a response to questions sent to its postal correspondence address.

The filing said the profit sharing arrangement was in return for services he provided ​to the company. Barrack also disclosed to the OGE a paid consulting role ​with the venture in 2024. The filing does not say whether or ⁠how much he was paid.

In a separate signed ethics agreement dated March 7, 2025, three weeks before his Senate confirmation hearing, Barrack listed ACD-TI Oakley among assets he would retain rather than sell.

The historic Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline, which for decades moved Iraqi crude to Syria's Mediterranean coast, faced sporadic shutdowns from the early 1980s and has been out of action since the US invasion of Iraq in 2003. Mothballed plans to revive it received new impetus this year when, under US attack, ​Iran restricted traffic through Hormuz, pushing oil prices higher.

Several people told Reuters in August the pipeline would take at least four years and cost $15 billion to build.

The idea of bringing TI Capital into the regional project was raised by ​Barrack in May at the Milken Institute ⁠Global Conference in Los Angeles, a third person with direct knowledge of the conversation told Reuters. The discussion, they added, took place on the sidelines of the event.

With the US war on Iran raging, Barrack and Ghandour also participated in an invite-only panel at the conference, where they discussed in more general terms the need for new energy supply lines in the Middle East, the person said.

A Milken Institute spokesperson declined to provide details of the panel discussion, saying it was closed to the media.

Barrack has engaged in business with Ghandour since at least 2020, when the two men created a $250 million blank-check SPAC that was dissolved after Barrack was arrested in 2021 on charges of acting as ⁠an unregistered agent of ​the United Arab Emirates. He was acquitted in 2022.

The Iraqi cabinet named TI Capital later in July as part of another consortium with UCC Holding and ConocoPhillips to assess the Akkas gas ​field, one of Iraq's largest undeveloped reserves. On its website, the firm claims involvement in projects at Syria's Tartous port, without providing details. Syria’s port authority did not reply to questions about TI Capital, and Reuters could not verify its role in Tartous. ConocoPhillips did not reply to a request for comment.

A person close to Barrack said the ambassador trusted Ghandour to help implement US President Donald ​Trump’s regional strategy of bringing Iraq and Syria closer to the US. “Ziad is the chosen man. Hand-picked by Barrack,” the person said.

The White House referred Reuters questions to the State Department.

items.title: NEWSLETTER: Are Democrats too confident about US midterms?
items.content_html:
Oct 8 (Reuters) - Democrats pushed further into deep Republican territory this week, adding US House districts President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024 to their midterm election target list, fueling talk of a Democratic, or "blue wave," victory on November 3.

But are Democrats in danger of misreading the size of the wave they believe is building?

Democrats are behaving ​less like a party fighting to take Congress from Republicans and more like one debating how large its future majority might be, even as ‌Trump is pursuing a 32-day campaign blitz to shore up Republican candidates hurt by high prices, the Iran war and his record-low approval ratings.

On Monday, the Democrats' US House campaign arm expanded its battlefield into solidly Republican districts in Kansas, Michigan, Oklahoma, Texas and Virginia, including a seat Trump carried by 24 points in 2024. Republicans and their allies have been diverting cash from competitive races to help candidates ​in once-safe seats now on the defensive.

Yet beneath the optimism, some worry Democrats might be getting carried away.

None of the party insiders, pollsters and analysts I spoke ​to doubt that Democrats will retake the House. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to retake the chamber. But several ⁠cautioned that a gain of 15 to 20 seats remains more likely than a historic rout.

The Senate remains a nail-biter. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip ​it, but most of their best opportunities are in Trump country and Republicans are running stronger than expected in states Democrats expected to be safer wins, including Maine, Michigan and ​New Hampshire.

Some are also haunted by opinion polls that have overstated Democratic strength in recent elections and the fact that voter enthusiasm does not always translate into turnout.

The signs of a potential Democratic wave are real enough. Whether that surge in support can deliver a commanding majority or a modest one – and whether it extends beyond the House – is the question that still hangs over November.

Follow Reuters/Ipsos polling on the president's approval ratings here.

Your questions: What are the most plausible paths for Democrats and Republicans to win control of the House and Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, and which races are most likely to determine the outcome?

Answer by Jason Lange, Politics Data Reporter

Democrats face an uphill fight to win the Senate, where they need to pick up four seats. They'd have to hold Michigan and New Hampshire – both tight races – while flipping four of ​six Republican-held seats in play: Alaska, Maine, ​North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa and Texas – the ⁠last two of which haven't elected Democrats to the Senate in over a decade.

Republicans face more pressure in the House, where their 218 members hold the smallest possible majority in the 435-seat chamber. About three dozen races nationwide are competitive. Democrats' best pickup chances ​include Republican-held seats in Nebraska's 2nd, New Jersey's 7th and California's 48th, where district boundaries were redrawn to favor Democrats. Democrats must ​also defend Ohio's 9th ⁠and North Carolina's 1st, both redrawn to favor Republicans.

The Trump administration pressed Moscow this week for more information about the death of a plague institute worker in Siberia. Russia's health regulator said on Wednesday there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out. Russian authorities said the 28-year-old laboratory worker died last Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in ⁠a case ​that has prompted international concern, including from Trump. Authorities initially placed around 200 people in quarantine.

items.title: US 30-year mortgage rate hits highest in nearly three years
items.content_html:
Oct 7 (Reuters) - The interest rate on the most common US home loan jumped last ‌week to its highest in almost three years, worsening affordability for buyers four weeks before elections that will decide if President Donald Trump's Republicans keep control of Congress.

The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage surged 19 basis points to 7.49% in the week ended October 2, the Mortgage ​Bankers Association said on Wednesday. It was last higher in November 2023.

Mortgage rates are tied closely to ​the yield on US 10-year Treasury notes, which earlier this week hit a 24-year high, driven ⁠by worries over inflationary pressures from soaring oil prices and data showing stronger US economic growth.

The cost of ​living is the top issue on Americans' minds as they decide how they will vote on November 3, a ​Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday showed, and is one reason why Trump's approval rating is at a record low of 32%.

Home borrowing rates are up about 1.4 percentage points since joint US-Israeli strikes against Iran began in late February, tracking a similar rise in the 10-year ​Treasury yield, which topped 5.3% on Monday.

Inflation is also on the rise, registering 3.4% in August by a measure ​that the Federal Reserve targets at 2%.

Fed policymakers have signaled they expect to follow their September interest-rate increase with another rate ‌hike by ⁠year's end, though markets are for now betting they will not move at their upcoming policy meeting at the end of October.

Asked by a reporter Wednesday about mortgage rates, Trump called Fed chairman Kevin Warsh "great," but added the rest of the board "would like to see the country do badly, in my opinion, because I think interest rates ​should come down."

US Treasury ​Secretary Scott Bessent, in ⁠the Oval Office with Trump, blamed inflation and high mortgage rates on the temporary shock from higher oil prices. "So once we get on the other side of this Iran ​conflict, (the) energy market is going to be well supplied, and we will move down ​towards the Fed's ⁠target and mortgage rates and the 10-year will come back down," Bessent said.

Mortgage loan applications fell 4.2% last week from the previous week, the MBA said on Wednesday, with refinancing applications dropping sharply. Overall application volumes are the lowest since February ⁠2025 ​and have fallen nearly 50% since January.

"Very few homeowners have an incentive ​to refinance at these rates, and the jump in borrowing costs has caused many potential borrowers to step back from the purchase market," ​said Joel Kan, the MBA’s deputy chief economist.

items.title: Trump voters are not pumped about voting in the midterms, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
Oct 8 (Reuters) - Voters who backed Democratic former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 are far more enthusiastic about casting ballots this November than ​those who supported President Donald Trump, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found, in a potential warning sign for Republicans heading into the midterm elections.

The six-day poll, completed Monday, also found that men were more enthusiastic ‌about voting and more certain to cast ballots than women, and that male voters showed signs of shifting toward Democrats. That could signal erosion in Republican support among a demographic that was a pillar of Trump's 2024 victory.

Some 48% of 2024 Harris voters said they were "very enthusiastic" about voting in the November 3 midterm elections, when control of both chambers of Congress is at stake. By comparison, just 30% of Trump voters said the same in the poll.

The findings add ​to evidence of an enthusiasm gap favoring Democrats and suggest potential cracks in the coalition that propelled Trump in 2024, when he won the popular vote. That coalition was fueled by ​strong support from men and gains among Hispanic voters and other demographic groups that shifted to the right in the 2024 election.

The poll also adds to ⁠a string of encouraging signs for Democrats, who are widely favored to win control of the House of Representatives and remain competitive in the fight for the Senate as Trump's approval ratings have ​slipped amid voter concerns about the cost of living and the war with Iran.

Republican strategist Charlie Gerow said the poll's findings raise the stakes for his party's turnout efforts, though he expects the enthusiasm gap ​to narrow as concerns about what he described as far-left Democrats gaining power motivate Republican voters.

"The enthusiasm has to be ginned up among Republicans because turnout is what's going to determine the outcome of these midterm elections," Gerow said.

While Trump voters overwhelmingly plan to vote Republican and Harris voters are similarly inclined to vote Democratic, the president's 2024 supporters are less decided, with 13% saying they aren't sure who to vote for in congressional elections, compared to 7% of ​Harris supporters who say the same.

The poll, which was conducted nationwide and surveyed 4,506 adults online, showed that just 32% of Americans approved of Trump's presidency, holding at a record ​low first marked in a September Reuters/Ipsos survey. The survey has a 2 percentage point margin of error.

Since taking office in January 2025, support for Trump has fallen across every major demographic group, including double-digit drops among Hispanics, ‌men, rural ⁠and suburban voters, people without college degrees and evangelical Christians.

One notable shift has come among men, a group Trump won in all three of his presidential campaigns, including by a 12-point margin in 2024, according to a Pew Research analysis.

When asked how they would vote in a congressional race if the elections were today, men in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll picked Democrats over Republicans, 43% to 39%. The four-point Democratic advantage was the widest of Trump's second term. Men consistently favored Republicans in 2025 but since August have mostly favored Democrats.

The warning signs for Republicans reflect growing voter concerns about the high cost of living amid a ​surge in gasoline and diesel prices following the ​war with Iran. Trump launched the Iran attacks in ⁠February, despite pledging during his campaign not to start new conflicts and to lower costs for consumers.

Cost of living is the top issue on Americans' minds as they decide how they will vote next month, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found. Voters cite democratic values as the second biggest issue, followed by immigration.

Republicans ​continue to hold an edge among older voters, a crucial bloc in midterm elections, when seniors have historically accounted for an outsized share of ​the electorate. Voters 50 and ⁠older still favor the Republican Party over the Democratic Party by 2 percentage points, 44% to 42%, though that was down from an 8-point Republican advantage in December.

Still, the enthusiasm gap looms large for Republicans.

Among all the voters in the poll who said they were enthusiastic, 62% said they were pumped about expressing opposition to Trump, compared to 36% who said they were eager to support the president.

Linda Rivera, a 46-year-old Trump voter in ⁠Pennsylvania, said that ​while she would probably vote Republican if she casts a ballot, she is frustrated with both parties and feels “neither enthusiastic ​or unenthusiastic” about voting next month.

Rivera, a respondent in the poll, said concerns about widespread voting fraud - which have been repeatedly fanned by Trump and his Republican allies without evidence - have added to her doubts about whether she will vote.

"I have lost ​faith in the voting process," she told Reuters. "I have lost faith in both parties. Not just one."

items.title: Florida asks court to force Meta to change Facebook, Instagram for teens
items.content_html:
Oct 7 (Reuters) - Florida ​asked a state judge on Wednesday to order changes to Instagram and Facebook to better ‌protect young users, pressing ahead with a lawsuit accusing parent Meta Platforms (META.O), opens new tab of harming teens after most states resolved similar claims through a sweeping settlement.

In a filing in a Pasco County court, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier asked for a temporary injunction ​forcing Meta to identify and remove users in the state under the age of 14 from ​those platforms, limit teens there to two hours a day across all apps and ⁠turn off features like autoplay and infinite scroll for them.

The filing asked that the changes be implemented immediately ​and be in place while the lawsuit moves forward.

A Meta spokesperson in a statement said after the company's ​settlement with nearly every other state, Florida should focus on getting other platforms to take action.

"The attorney general should be using taxpayer resources to get YouTube and TikTok to empower parents and protect teens in Florida. We regret that he has chosen ​instead to pursue a meritless preliminary injunction years into the litigation," the spokesperson said.

Florida's lawsuit against Meta, which ​accuses the company of knowingly engineering its platforms to be addictive for young users and misleading consumers about its safety, was ‌one ⁠of dozens of similar lawsuits filed by states across the country.

In August, Meta reached settlements with 48 of the other states and Washington, DC, agreeing to pay up to $18 billion and make changes for teen users of its platforms.

Meta has said it works hard to keep teens safe on its platforms, and the company denied wrongdoing ​in agreeing to settle. The ​total payout represents about ⁠three to four months of profit and about one month of revenue for Meta.

Uthmeier, a Republican, opted not to join the settlement and proceed with his lawsuit.

Florida said ​in the filing that the settlement amounted to a “mere slap on the wrist, ​will be cynically ⁠viewed as the cost of doing business, and in any event will not prevent this kind of behavior going forward.”

The changes Uthmeier's filing seeks are more stringent than those the company agreed to as part of that settlement, ⁠as they ​would cut off teens' access to messaging after their time ​limits are hit and bar the company from showing them advertisements.

The changes Meta agreed to make as part of the settlement are an ​indication these changes are possible, Uthmeier's office argued.
